Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor.
  • Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague.
  • In a recent development, examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings. Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do.

So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle.

Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt.

In a recent development, examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also, which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI tech giant although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday, which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name.

In a recent development, “Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden, who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming, told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward.

When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference.

In a recent development, “We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” mentioned Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. “So we have to look for something unexpected.

According to recent reports, given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face, the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt.

Another more recent upstart that caught his attention is Flapping Airplanes, an AI research lab that raised a $1 billion Series A last month.

“It’s super playful, but you remember it, and you have this visual,” he stated. Plus, it’s not the kind of name one’s lawyer finds is already taken by a competitor.

Recent findings suggest that the AI boom is also often characterized as a period in which companies are building the foundational layer of a technology that will fundamentally transform our lives for decades to come. Given this mindset, it’s perhaps predictable that we’re seeing a plethora of names with themes tied to building and industry.

Industry observers note that foden points to Databricks as one of the more longstanding representatives of this naming approach. Its brand evokes the notion of digital data as one small component of a massive building endeavor.

According to recent reports, but newer upstarts are onto this trend as well. There’s an abundance of recently founded companies with “foundation” in their name, for instance, including Foundation Health, Foundation Industries, Foundational Industries, Foundational and Foundation.

Another recent example with an industrial, maker vibe is Blacksmith, a cloud infrastructure startup founded in 2024 that’s pulled in more than $100 million this year.

Dating app Rivet looks like a more unusual sector match for an industrial name. The two-year-old startup runs a platform in which volunteer matchmakers pick matches for daters.

Nuclear startup Standard Nuclear, meanwhile, reads like a twist on Gilded Age industrial giant Standard Oil.

In a recent development, there’s also a continuing effort to add a humanizing element to AI and robotics technologies. After all, no one wants to patronize a company called “AI-Enabled Robotics Overlord Who Will Soon Be Taking Your Job.”.

It’s not just newer startups applying this tactic. Startups have a long history of going with popular first names as brands. And of course Anthropic has secured massive market share  of late with a chatbot and coder named Claude.

According to recent reports, newer funded startups with first name-based brands include Theo, Henry, Clara and Mira, among others. Then there’s Humans&, an AI startup that’s taking a different route to attempt a humanizing brand.

Of course, nowadays it’s not even necessary to confer with a human when generating naming ideas. You can just ask AI for suggestions.

Per Benedini, the technology’s not there yet.

Industry observers note that “We still use AI to see what it comes up with, and it’s like 99% garbage,” he stated. Moreover, selecting a name is only the first step — one must also determine if it’s available for use.

According to recent reports, still, it’s early days. Perhaps in the future it will be AI naming AI companies to appeal to other AI agents. But hopefully there will still be a role for us to play going forward.

Sample set was limited to startups in English-speaking countries. ↩.

Tech Report: End of Crypto Trading? How AI Replaces Ones Who Pumped Bitcoin (BTC)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: U

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the “pump” trade could be taken to fresh extremes.
  • All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing problems with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.
  • Automation is not necessarily a newly introduced occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the “pump” trade could be taken to fresh extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing problems with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a newly introduced occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Industry observers note that coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

In a recent development, AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Recent findings suggest that also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

In a recent development, are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Institutions are (and will continue to be) an important source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

In a recent development, institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

It has been revealed that the future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it declared two years ago.

Recent findings suggest that rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the fresh fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

In a recent development, certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
  • The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer.
  • Industry observers note that nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Industry observers note that nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Recent findings suggest that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

It has been revealed that fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

According to recent reports, “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

#133403. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1041 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that slowMist states five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that slowMist states five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

According to recent reports, the reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery strategy has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a latest wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist states the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

According to recent reports, the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Consumers with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its initiative for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

#133402. Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (908 w)

Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am.
  • Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving.
  • Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am.

Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

Airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a newly introduced Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

Oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Sources indicate that decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

Recent findings suggest that reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Sources indicate that pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

According to recent reports, potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

In a recent development, trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

According to recent reports, live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

In a recent development, friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a latest meal.

Specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or remarked.

Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

According to recent reports, “We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

It has been revealed that black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items revealed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the New York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

According to recent reports, don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the Latest York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

It has been revealed that don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

According to recent reports, don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot indicates that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, via his X account on Sunday, Nov. 22, Davis asked Cardano CEO Charles Hoskinson about intends to grow adoption on the network. With his huge crypto audience, the trader said many customers often ask him what has been holding Cardano back. As a result, he inquired why the protocol has failed to attract customers and capture meaningful market share. Compared with newer crypto networks like Solana, the analyst pointed out that Cardano’s daily active users and DeFi activity appear significantly low.

The Cardano founder suddenly emerged online on Sunday and responded to the celebrated trader. Hoskinson highlighted possible reasons, though with cautionary remarks. His answer hinted that a crypto network’s adoption is not determined by price, but by usage and transactions – indicators of real adoption.

Sources indicate that according to Hoskinson, Cardano powers immense real-world on-chain use cases, financial applications, and tokenization utilities whose values are not directly measured by ADA price. He said Cardano’s infrastructure and applications are stronger than before, regardless of the ADA price.

He maintained that price doesn’t always show a network’s full capabilities. He added that different networks are on their own journeys and priorities, so comparing Solana with Cardano’s situation doesn’t make sense.

Despite Cardano launching four years earlier, its daily active owners are roughly 1% of Solana’s. Today, ADA trades at $0.1547, 95.3% down from its $3.09 peak reached five years ago in 2021.

In a recent development, the question above about ADA and SOL highlights the battle for leadership in the crypto space. The two assets have emerged as two of the most popular chains, each with their own strengths and limitations.

  • Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo.
  • It has been revealed that one candidate improves the slides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect?

Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice.

It has been revealed that one candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor.

In a recent development, AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it.

Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words.

But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper.

An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job?

According to recent reports, I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone claims they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate.

CoderPad offers an interview environment where candidates use AI on realistic tasks while interviewers watch how they prompt, evaluate and revise the output. That gives employers a practical way to observe a skill candidates will increasingly need on the job.

According to recent reports, I’d give every finalist the same flawed acquisition memo, the same source documents and access to the same AI tools. Then I’d ask what they would verify before sending the memo to a client. One might catch the double-counted revenue. Another might go further and work out whether the corrected numbers change the price we should offer. The most revealing moment may come when the tool confidently insists its original calculation was right. What does the candidate do then?

Lattice lets managers use AI to draft reviews from goals, feedback and meeting notes. Synq, formerly Gloat, says its software can build and run a review cycle from a plain-English instruction. These tools make it easier to collect and summarize evidence. That makes the choice of what to collect more consequential.

  • In a post on X commemorating the Bitwise XRP ETF's first anniversary, Bitwise remarked the fund had recorded over $667 million in net inflows and had more than $376 million in assets under management (AUM) since launch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bitwise XRP ETF traded an average of about $14 million a day over its first year on the market, resulting in over $3.5 billion in total trading volume, according to Bitwise.

In a post on X commemorating the Bitwise XRP ETF's first anniversary, Bitwise remarked the fund had recorded over $667 million in net inflows and had more than $376 million in assets under management (AUM) since launch.

Bitwise's XRP ETF started trading on Nov. 20, 2025, on NYSE Arca. It trades under the same ticker as the cryptocurrency it holds, XRP.

Investors can use the ETF's shares to track the price of the token through their brokerage accounts. The fund holds the XRP on behalf of investors. At launch, the ETF charged a 0.34% annual management fee. It also offered a fee waiver for the first $500 million in assets for the first month.

According to recent reports, the $3.5 billion in trading volume is the total value of purchases and sales of the ETF's shares. This means the same ETF shares could trade repeatedly. If an investor sells their shares to another investor, that transaction increases trading volume. But the total XRP held in the fund doesn't change in that case.

On the other hand, the $667 million in net inflows represents the total dollar value of fresh shares issued over the past year minus redeemed shares.

AUM represents the total dollar value of a fund's assets at a specific moment. Since the fund's total assets are valued in dollars, AUM can fall below cumulative net inflows if the price of XRP declines, even as investors continue to put money into the fund.

In a recent development, the quarterly report filed by Bitwise with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) highlights the impact of investor demand and XRP's price on the fund over the past year.

The net asset value of the fund increased from $299.1 million at the end of June to $614.9 million at the end of September.

Sources indicate that over $315.7 million was added to the fund's net assets during that quarter. Just over half of that $315.7 million came from new share creations.

It has been revealed that the fund issued new shares with a total dollar value of $210.7 million. It also redeemed $32.8 million in shares during that quarter. So that left about $178 million in net new creations.

The fund issued 13.75 million shares and redeemed 2.42 million shares.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

According to recent reports, more specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he claims that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a latest sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

Industry observers note that the now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the organization has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a latest reality: many more people among them are at risk.
  • “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
  • That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a latest reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

Sources indicate that but now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown indicates, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”.

Recent findings suggest that huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of manufacturer secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

In a recent development, and typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”.

Recent findings suggest that what’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

Recent findings suggest that “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter stated. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”.

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown mentioned.

It has been revealed that “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”.

Industry observers note that carpenter noted a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”.

It has been revealed that it also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he remarked, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the manufacturer.

Brown added that firm culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter mentioned.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown noted. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”.

  • The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.
  • Sources indicate that in a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:46 pm.

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

Sources indicate that in a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold newly introduced frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He mentioned that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr noted.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”.

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS mentioned in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation.

It has been revealed that spaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

According to recent reports, in August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX noted at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC stated it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”.

Tech Report: How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token.
  • Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine.
  • They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor declared gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Sources indicate that setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Customers who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

Sources indicate that the gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

It has been revealed that gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

It has been revealed that every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example reveals the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is revealed, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

According to recent reports, the docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

Recent findings suggest that A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said on X that the company is repurchasing stock in the fourth quarter because investors are overlooking the potential of the payments business for AI agents.

"Good to take advantage of market dislocations," said Armstrong.

Industry observers note that the firm is buying back stock using funds previously authorized for repurchases. He didn't specify the number of COIN shares, the price or the amount spent.

In a recent development, at the start of the quarter, Coinbase had $1.96 billion left to repurchase stock. Over the prior three months, it repurchased 37,995 shares for a total cost of $5.3 million, at an average price of $139.91. All repurchases occurred in August, according to its third-quarter report.

Sources indicate that coinbase's board of directors initially authorized stock buybacks of up to $1 billion in October 2024. A year later, the buyback authorization was doubled. The company also received an option to repurchase some outstanding debt.

The board increased the buyback limit again in January 2026, bringing the total authorization to $4 billion.

Some buybacks have been carried out to cancel stock issued as employee compensation. By the end of September, the company had repurchased 10.2 million Class A shares and canceled more than 85% of the stock issued for employee compensation since the fourth quarter of 2024. This is according to an earnings presentation.

Armstrong envisions a scenario where crypto and AI are involved in different aspects of the same transaction.

For example, AI agents might help users make financial decisions and follow their instructions. Then, a crypto network may be used to transfer funds.

Coinbase wants to provide accounts, payment services, and marketplaces for humans and AI agents to use.

Sources indicate that "With AI, everybody has a private banker in your pocket that can help you make better financial decisions," Armstrong posted on Nov. 25.

According to recent reports, coinbase added its wallet and payment services to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments. This offers a way for developers to build agents on Amazon and allow the software to discover paid services. Agents can make small payments when necessary.

Now Armstrong is inviting developers to add their specialized AI models to Agentic.Market.

According to Armstrong, an AI agent can choose which specialist to hire for a task based on its capabilities and price. Coinbase provides the platform where agents can find specialists and pay them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech organization Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”.

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

#133392. Your AI Startup’s Exit Is Being Shaped By The Deals You Sign Today

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1082 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crunchbase ↗ Open Full Page

Your AI Startup’s Exit Is Being Shaped By The Deals You Sign Today

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever.
  • Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.
  • It has been revealed that when everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Aaron Rubin and Greg Volkmar.

Sources indicate that valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever. In the financings our firm has worked on so far in 2026, AI companies raised at median pre-money valuations up to 2.5 times those of non-AI companies from seed through Series C.

Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.

It has been revealed that when everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry. Some of those terms will later slow a sale, add cost and erode value. The key is making sure you take long enough to consider what a deal does to your exit before you sign.

Recent findings suggest that take license-and-hire deals, where a buyer licenses your technology and hires your team instead of acquiring the manufacturer. They’ve become more common in AI, and the National Venture Capital Association has responded by updating its model charter. In 2025, it added an optional investor approval right over these deals, and sign-off by the board, including the investors’ directors, was enough to satisfy it.

In a recent development, the November 2026 enhancement requires a vote of the preferred stockholders instead. Investors are often reluctant to use an approval right to block a deal. But it puts them at the negotiating table when an offer arrives, with a voice in how the proceeds are split between retention packages for the team and the cap table.

The stakes are higher when an investor is also a strategic partner. Nvidia and its NVentures investment arm alone have invested in more than 260 startups since the beginning of 2024, including 121 this year alone, Crunchbase data highlights.

According to recent reports, strategic capital often comes tied to compute, cloud or distribution agreements. Those agreements can carry exclusivity, change-of-control and right-of-first-negotiation terms, and a right of first negotiation can force you to put a competing bidder on ice while you talk to your strategic investor first.

It has been revealed that be realistic about your leverage. Terms from the hottest AI rounds get cited as “market,” but what you can get depends on how much investors want your deal. Spend your negotiating capital on the few provisions that will matter most in a sale instead of trying to optimize on marginal topics.

An AI manufacturer’s most valuable assets are often the hardest to diligence.

It has been revealed that start with data. A buyer will want to know where your training data came from and whether your contractual rights cover how you use it and how the buyer plans to use it. Publicly available data isn’t necessarily licensed data. And permission to use a customer’s data to serve that customer doesn’t always cover training models for everyone else. If you fine-tuned on customer data under contracts that limit its use to serving those customers, a buyer may not be able to fold your models into its own products. The buyer may ask for a special indemnity, a larger escrow or a lower purchase price.

Your code gets similar scrutiny. In our deals, investors, and especially acquirers, now ask how much of the codebase was written with AI tools and whether those tools pulled in copyleft or commercially licensed code. We tell clients to audit their code regularly and fix challenges as they surface. It makes that diligence conversation far easier.

Industry observers note that compute and model-provider contracts raise a different problem: a buyer may inherit a commitment it doesn’t want. Minimum-spend commitments, reserved capacity and exclusivity terms generally stay with the manufacturer in a sale. A buyer with its own GPUs may have no use for three more years of your reserved capacity, and it will factor the remaining payments into its offer.

All of this is easier to fix at the negotiating table than in the middle of a buyer’s diligence.

Sources indicate that • Map who decides on a sale. Know which board and investor approvals it would trigger, including any approval right over a license-and-hire deal.

Recent findings suggest that • Track your data and code rights. Record data sources and use restrictions and audit AI-generated code periodically.

• Stress-test your infrastructure commitments. Run cloud, GPU and model-provider obligations against slower growth and a sale.

According to recent reports, • Keep strategic rights narrow. Limit the scope, duration and triggers of any right of first offer or negotiation you give a strategic investor.

Sources indicate that • Read commercial contracts with an exit in mind. Check the change-of-control and termination rights before you sign.

According to recent reports, few founders are thinking about a sale when they close a seed round or sign their first GPU contract. You don’t have to predict the exit. You do have to know what you’re giving up each time you sign, so the speed that got you funded doesn’t cost you flexibility when the right acquisition offer arrives.

Aaron Rubin is a partner in Gunderson Dettmer’s Strategic Transactions & Licensing group and a leader of the firm’s artificial intelligence practice. He advises AI companies on strategic partnerships, technology and data licensing, and the development, commercialization, and deployment of AI products and services. His practice spans complex commercial transactions, intellectual property and data rights, and the evolving legal and regulatory issues shaping the AI industry. He also advises leading investors in industry-defining AI financings, including investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks.

Greg Volkmar is head of Gunderson Dettmer’s New York corporate group and co-chairs the firm’s growth equity practice. For more than 20 years, Volkmar has focused on advising early- and late-stage technology and life science companies through financings, corporate governance, and securities law matters. He is also a trusted advisor to leading venture capital, private equity and crossover funds on their US and global investment activities, such as equity and debt financings, mergers and acquisitions, and secondary liquidity transactions, as well as fund formation needs.

#133391. Breaking: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1102 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself?
  • According to recent reports, now, the manufacturer has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business.
  • Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

According to recent reports, now, the manufacturer has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.

In a recent development, “We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano noted. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the tech giant day to day.

According to recent reports, the team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading debuts like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a fresh level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Right now, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the firm intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

In a recent development, supertake’s customers’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.

“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he states. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”.

“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.

“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

In a recent development, to address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team states it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.

Sources indicate that “We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” notes Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”.

Access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders remarked they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.
